solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Might this produce me a car — or an image?

definitions.text: Might this produce me a car — or an image?

parts.words: Might this produce me a car — or an image?
parts.note: a darkened box or room with a lens throws a picture of the outside scene onto a wall; the first word of its name is also a jumble of 'me a car'

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a gadget might conjure up a car for them, or merely a picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on the first word of the answer being a rearrangement of 'me a car', but the second word is not built from the clue, so the whole reads as a cryptic definition of an image-projecting device.
explanation.definitionFit: This optical device projects an image of its surroundings through a small hole or lens onto a screen.

clue.text: Talisman joins odious campaign of flattery

parts.note: a charm is a lucky amulet or talisman
odious means offensive, disgusting

explanation.surface: A lucky amulet is paired with a nasty push to win people over.
explanation.definitionFit: A charm offensive is a concerted effort to win favour by being pleasant, a flattery campaign.

clue.text: Yank's admission of error — admirably put right — no liar involved

indicators.note: put right says the remaining letters are set in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters removed by 'no ... involved'

explanation.surface: An American owns up to a mistake, put admirably and honestly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no liar involved' removes L, I, A, R from ADMIRABLY, leaving DMABY, which 'put right' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: The American slang phrase is a casual way of conceding that one made a mistake, saying sorry.

clue.text: Where meat may be on the turn, putrefy, and is dumped on small lake

definitions.text: Where meat may be on the turn

indicators.note: in a down clue the earlier pieces are dumped on top of the lake, coming before it

parts.note: to rot is to putrefy
Erie is one of the Great Lakes

explanation.surface: Meat that has gone off is thrown onto a little pond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the turn' suggests meat going bad; it means meat turning on a spit.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotisserie is a rotating spit on which meat is roasted, so the meat turns there.

clue.text: Pompous fanatic turns up in front of oyster bar

indicators.note: front of takes the first letter of the shellfish
in means the turned word goes inside the other pieces

parts.note: a rod is a bar

indicators.note: in a down clue turns up means the word for a fanatic is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a nut is a fanatic, an enthusiast

explanation.surface: A self-important zealot shows up at an oyster bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oyster bar' reads as a restaurant, but it splits: the shellfish gives only its first letter and 'bar' is a rod.
explanation.definitionFit: Orotund describes a voice or style that is booming and grandiloquent, pompous and showy.

clue.text: Flyers taking relatives (singly and as a group) over Sweden

indicators.note: in a down clue over means the relatives sit above Sweden, so before it

parts.note: sis is short for sister, a single relative, as 'singly' indicates
kin is one's relatives taken as a group
S is the international vehicle registration letter for Sweden

explanation.surface: Birds flying over Sweden with their family members.
explanation.definitionFit: Siskins are small finches, songbirds that fly, so they are flyers.

clue.text: Release article in Le Monde to fit the bill

parts.note: un is the French indefinite article, as might appear in the French newspaper Le Monde
to do is to suffice, as in 'that will do'

explanation.surface: A newspaper story is let loose because it suits the requirement.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo a knot or fastening is to loosen or free it, letting it go.

clue.text: Made mental note: 'Rusticate student to gain expiation'

indicators.note: made, as in made into something new, says the letters are rearranged

parts.note: L is a learner, the student driver's plate

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to expel a pupil as a form of penance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rusticate' (to send a student down from university) removes L from MENTAL NOTE, and 'Made' rearranges the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Atonement is making amends for wrongdoing, which is exactly what expiation means.

clue.text: Grouse — rubbery thing — in a dish

parts.note: to grouse is to complain, to beef
a wellington is a rubber boot

explanation.surface: A game bird and a rubber object end up together on a plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' suggests the game bird but is the verb to complain; a wellington (welly) is a British rubber boot.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a fillet steak baked in pastry, a classic main course.

clue.text: Bird's uncomfortable neckwear?

definitions.meaning: a huge seabird of the southern oceans
in Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner the sailor must wear the shot bird around his neck, hence a burden one cannot shake off

explanation.surface: A question about why a bird might have an awkward collar.
explanation.definitionFit: The great seabird is the creature hung round the Mariner's neck, so its name stands for a heavy, unwanted burden.

clue.text: Slacker among the basses?

definitions.meaning: an idler who lives off others' work, like the male bee
a low continuous note, such as the bass pipes of bagpipes, sounds among the low parts

explanation.surface: A lazy chorister is spotted hiding in the bass section.
explanation.definitionFit: The idle male bee gives a word for a loafer, and the same word names a sustained low bass note or pipe.

clue.text: Writing about verse forms

indicators.note: about means the writing goes round the outside of the verse

parts.note: MS is the abbreviation for manuscript, a piece of writing
an ode is a lyric poem, a piece of verse

explanation.surface: An essay discussing the different types of poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'verse forms' reads as one phrase, but 'verse' is the inner piece and 'forms' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Modes are manners or styles of doing something, so they are kinds or ways, like forms.

clue.text: Part of shotgun I tested for detachment

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A shotgun put through trials by a military detachment.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition took in 'for'; it is only the link joining wordplay to definition, so the definition is 'detachment' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: In military language a detachment is a group of soldiers sent off on a task, a body of troops.

clue.text: Brownie's after pennies in old money

indicators.note: after puts the sprite behind the pennies in the answer

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for pence or pennies
a brownie is a helpful household sprite of folklore, so a kind of elf; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A young Girl Guide (a Brownie) collecting coins in pre-decimal currency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brownie' suggests the junior Girl Guides, but here it is the goblin of folklore.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelf is an old-fashioned, rather disparaging word for wealth or riches.

clue.text: How to acquire ales in second-hand market?

parts.note: to jumble the word 'sale' is to mix its letters, producing ales

explanation.surface: Wondering how to buy beer at a second-hand sale.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumble sale is a British charity sale of used goods, like a rummage sale.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a sale of donated used goods, often for charity, a market for second-hand items.

clue.text: Deficient padre given notice — dimwit!

indicators.note: deficient means the priest's title lacks something, here its last letter

parts.note: a padre is a priest, addressed as father
an ad, an advertisement, is a notice

explanation.surface: An inadequate chaplain is sacked and insulted as an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given notice' looks like dismissal, but 'notice' is simply an advertisement.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupid person is called a thickhead or numbskull, which is what this insult means.

clue.text: In a truck, sit changing gear for practice

indicators.note: changing says these letters alter their order

explanation.surface: Someone sits in a truck changing into their training kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing gear' looks like a driving phrase, but 'changing' is the anagram signal and 'gear' starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tracksuit is the loose outfit athletes wear while training, clothing for practice.

clue.text: Steady with concertina — no case

indicators.note: no says the case is taken away from the instrument's name

parts.note: a concertina is a small accordion, informally a squeezebox
a box is a case or container

explanation.surface: Someone tries to keep a concertina stable once it is out of its case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steady' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: a regular boyfriend or girlfriend.
explanation.definitionFit: A steady is a regular partner, and a squeeze is informal slang for one's girlfriend or boyfriend.

clue.text: Girl with mount in escape attempt

parts.note: Eva is a girl's name
Sion is an alternative spelling of Mount Zion in Jerusalem

explanation.surface: A girl on horseback trying to get away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mount' suggests a horse; it is the biblical hill.
explanation.definitionFit: Evasion is the act of dodging or escaping, as in evading capture or a question.

clue.text: Party with only bottled beer? Impossible!

parts.note: if beer comes only in bottles there is no can
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A party with nothing but bottled beer is unthinkable.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase is a flat refusal, meaning a thing just cannot be done.

clue.text: Ring road in Baltimore suffering disruption? Let me out!

indicators.note: suffering disruption says the city's letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, the letters released by 'Let ... out'

explanation.surface: Stuck in a traffic jam on a Baltimore bypass, someone pleads to be let out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let me out' is both the motorist's plea and the instruction to remove those two letters before rearranging. The London Orbital is the M25 motorway ringing London.
explanation.definitionFit: An orbital is a road that circles a city, as the M25 goes round London.

clue.text: In open, Toughie team gets saturated

indicators.note: in means the team goes inside the word for open

parts.note: overt means open, not hidden
the setters of the Toughie refer to themselves as we

explanation.surface: Playing outdoors, the puzzle team gets soaked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toughie team' is the setter speaking of themselves as WE.
explanation.definitionFit: Overwet means soaked through, too wet, so drenched or saturated.

clue.text: Reason for a drink?

definitions.meaning: as in 'for the ... of', a purpose or reason

explanation.surface: Someone asks what excuse there is for a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is purpose, as in 'for goodness' sake'; the other is Japanese rice wine, rice-based alcohol.

clue.text: High point seen regularly in Salcombe

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter, here the even ones, of the place name

explanation.surface: A summit spotted now and then in the Devon resort of Salcombe.
explanation.definitionFit: The acme is the peak or pinnacle of achievement, the highest point.

clue.text: Put away school's report

indicators.note: report means the school's name is spoken aloud

parts.note: Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: A pupil is sent off after a bad school report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'report' suggests a school report but asks for a word heard; Eton is a famous English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: To put away food is informal for consuming it, so the past participle fits 'put away'.

clue.text: Capital letters missing from laman's untutred aricle expunding taewondo; deal with them!

indicators.note: deal with them asks the solver to reorder the missing letters

parts.words: letters missing from laman's untutred aricle expunding taewondo
parts.note: the words should read layman's untutored article expounding taekwondo, so the missing letters are Y, O, T, O and K

explanation.surface: A misspelt beginner's article about a martial art.
explanation.walkthrough: Each mangled word lacks one letter: Y, O, T, O, K. 'deal with them!' asks for these to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Tokyo is the capital city of Japan.

clue.text: No fun aimlessly mixing handful of lentils

indicators.note: aimlessly mixing says the remaining letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters removed by 'No'

explanation.surface: No pleasure in idly stirring a fistful of lentils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No fun' removes F, U, N from HANDFUL, leaving HADL, which 'aimlessly mixing' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Dhal is the Indian word for split pulses, especially lentils, and the dish made from them.

clue.text: Victor's cry of pain? Provide support

parts.note: Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet; the 's is 'has'
ouch is what one cries when hurt

explanation.surface: A man named Victor yelps in pain and asks for help.
explanation.definitionFit: To vouch for someone is to back them up or guarantee them, giving support.

clue.text: Course correction for watermen conveying king

indicators.note: conveying means the shuffled letters carry the king inside them
a correction for the word puts its letters right, rearranged

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: Boatmen are told to alter their route to carry a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'correction for' rearranges WATERMEN into NEWMARET, and 'conveying' puts K inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Newmarket is a famous English racecourse in Suffolk, the home of British horse racing.

clue.text: Scouse, perhaps, subject of tittle-tattle

definitions.meaning: Scouse is the dialect of Liverpool, an example of a town's speech

explanation.surface: The Liverpool accent is a favourite topic of gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: Scouse is the accent and dialect of Liverpool, so read literally it is the speech of a city.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a person or event everybody is discussing, the centre of gossip.
